title: Labour’s EU reset deal will be ‘floor not ceiling’, says Burnham cabinet ally

text: Labour’s EU reset deal will be a “floor not a ceiling”, according to a close cabinet ally of Andy Burnham, who says the UK has been a “cork bobbing on the tides of history” because of the power lost by Brexit.

Douglas Alexander, the Scottish secretary, will tell a conference in Italy on Friday that the government cannot deliver the major change Britain needs “without changing our relationship with Europe. When the status quo is not working, you don’t stand still. You move forward. When the status quo is broken, you don’t ignore it. You fix it.”

Alexander will make his speech a day after the government laid the bill to enact the new food and drink deal struck with the EU. The legislation gives ministers the power to strike even closer future ties, though stopping short of Labour’s red lines on free movement and the single market.
His speech will make him the first cabinet minister to explicitly endorse going further than Burnham’s reset deal last week rather than urging caution.
The former trade minister, who has long been a political ally of Burnham, will say he expects Labour to mount a better case for European unity than the one made in 2016 at the referendum.
“In difficult times, people want a vision of a better future, not just better management of the present,” Alexander will say. “And in political terms, that requires emotion as well as evidence.

“In 2016, the government of the day brought spreadsheets to a fight about who we are. This government won’t make that mistake, because this government understands that politics is about passion as well as pragmatism, and understands the animating importance of hope in influencing today and shaping tomorrow.”
Alexander’s enthusiastic endorsement of closer European ties makes him an outlier among cabinet colleagues, several of whom have expressed public caution at going faster than the public.
He will say the UK is “now living through an era of great power rivalry, and that it will largely define the decade ahead”.
”The answer, for the whole of Britain, and for Scotland, is interdependence not independence, advancing politics that gives people back control by giving them back a future.”

The government put what it is calling the “cutting costs bill” before parliament on Thursday, beginning the legislation to put the deal into law after it was agreed with the EU last Friday – though the deal to ease access for food and drink exports will not come into force until 2028, with the emissions trading deal to follow that year.

The text of the deal published on Thursday confirms that although the UK will have input in designing future agriculture, food and emissions rules, it will not have a final vote. It will also contain a so-called Farage clause – a financial penalty if the UK or EU reneges on the deals over the next decade.

But UK negotiators said the deal showed there were significant wins in securing consultation with the EU at every stage of new rules being designed, rather than just at their final implementation, which had been the EU’s original position.
Hamish Falconer, the Cabinet Office minister and lead negotiator for the deal, wrote to opposition parties, including Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage, on Thursday challenging them to support the bill.

“The status quo is not working. Brexit has done more harm than good,” the letter said. “A vote against this bill is a vote to maintain costly bureaucracy, to keep trade barriers in place and to hold back businesses looking to scale up into Europe.”

The bill will enact the food and drink and emissions deals but retain powers for future deals to be struck – including one to create a common single market for energy which both sides have begun work on. The bill is a “framework bill” that leaves room for any future deals to be designated as “partnership treaties” and enacted via the same legislation – though it excludes rejoining the single market or customs union, or fully rejoining the EU.
The formal terms of a new youth mobility deal are still to be published, which will contain the final number of youth visas that will be offered to individual EU member states, totalling 100,000.
That deal will be tied to the food and drink deal, meaning that the closer trading ties will be cancelled if the UK reneges on the youth visas.
The 80 page legal text of the food and drink agreement outlines the rules for a new common trading area, to which the “UK shall dynamically align and simultaneously apply”.

Under the deal, the UK will have a “consultative” role in EU legislation but “no voting rights” even in discussion on emergencies such as disease outbreaks. UK officials said that the UK would have a formal role in designing the rules and the ability to seek independent arbitration, but conceded it would not have final vote.
The deal also allows the EU to introduce temporary laws to “protect” the bloc in the event it cannot reach agreement with the UK on a particular issue to dynamically align.

Experts in the UK and member states will be “informally consulted”, which may not satisfy food industry bodies that have argued that British regulators should be involved in all the technical meetings before the drafting of EU laws.

EU sources have made clear that the adoption of the three main elements of last Friday’s reset will not take place until a separate agreement is reached on the level of tuition fees EU students will pay at UK universities. UK officials have firmly denied that is the case and insist the matters are separate.
But one senior EU diplomat said the agreements “will not materialise” without a deal on home rates on tuition fees within six months and there was “solidarity” among member states on this point.

A second senior EU diplomat said the UK’s handling of the tuition fees issue had been “toxic” and reminded them of the approach under previous governments led by Boris Johnson and Theresa May. “Nobody has charged British students [studying in the EU] any more since Brexit. This is why everybody is finding it a bit rich of them to insist on this.”
